title: The global order must be rebuilt without the fantasy of equality
subtitle: China, The West, and the real reason globalization failed
author: Tongdong Bai
introduction: After the world wars, there was widespread agreement in the West: national interest should bow to universal rights and the equality of all peoples. But Tongdong Bai, Chair of Philosophy at Fudan University in China, argues that this ideal rests on fantasy psychology: the belief that human beings can love and care about everybody equally. Real love grows from intimate bonds. Extended equally across all humanity, it becomes a bloodless, rationalistic simulacrum. Instead, we must accept we are self-interested and that we love our kin more than we do outsiders. But that does not mean that anyone who is not us, is against us. We must care for all, only, unequally.
body:
Globalization is in crisis, and this should come as no surprise at all. For globalization has been led by nation-states. A nation-state, by definition, will do whatever it takes for its own national interest. Globalization, in contrast, means going beyond nation-states and national interests. But if globalization is led by nation-states, it can only be maintained for as long as national leaders consider it beneficial to their states’ interests. When they lose faith in this, globalization will be in peril. When the Cold War ended, the United States became the leader of globalization. When it thought that it benefited from this leadership position, it was happy to offer the service of leadership. However, in the past decade or more, the US has lost faith in this, and so has begun rejecting its leadership role and accusing other states of taking a free ride from its service and even stealing from it. This sudden change is almost comical, like when, in the movie Casablanca, the French police chief Captain Renault, who is involved in a gambling den, comes under pressure from some Nazi officers and says, “I’m shocked, shocked to find that gambling is going on in here.”

If the world’s top economy refuses to maintain the global order, what about the second-top economy, China? If we consult the history of new national powers rising, it doesn’t give us confidence. For when a nation-state is rising, it tends to demand more for its own national interest. The rest of the world, consisting of nation-states as well, obviously doesn’t want to give in. The result is often war, including the First and Second World Wars.

The West, especially the “old Europe” or Western Europe, having learned the lesson from these wars, tried to go beyond nation-states by way of cosmopolitanism. A more aggressive form of the cosmopolitan attempt is guided by the idea that human rights override sovereignty, and it leads Western countries to intervene abroad, with many human rights violations and even crude oppressions and mass killings. Interventions in the past two decades, such as in Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, and Syria, however, seem to create new and even greater miseries than those they were intended to eliminate. To make things right seems to demand so much of Western countries that, often, they can only give lip-service to the principle that human rights override sovereignty, leading to skepticism and cynicism. A less aggressive form of cosmopolitanism, such as the formation of the European Union and the creation of a world market, doesn’t seem to do too well, either. For it leads to serious domestic problems, such as rising economic inequality, and political instability that is caused by the failure to assimilate a large group of people with different cultures and religions. All of this has led to the rise of right-wing populism in the West.

Are we doomed, then, to keep repeating radical swings between nationalism and cosmopolitanism? These two alternatives seem to be all we have come up with since the arrival of modernity, or, should we say, European or Western modernity. But is there another modernity? I will say yes. About 2,000 years before European modernity, China entered a transitional period, from 770 BCE to 221 BCE. Before this transition, the old “world order”—the world known to the Chinese—was built on a hierarchy of nobility, in which noble men of each level ran their fiefdoms with some autonomy, and through the pyramid of nobility, a large empire was divided into small, close-knit feudal communities, like in Europe in the Middle Ages. But this order collapsed, and through wars of all against all, large, populous, well-connected, plebeianized societies of strangers emerged. Thus, a few de facto sovereign states arose in the “world.” This transition may be a forerunner of the European transition to modernity. Common to both transitions is the need to address three key political issues in this new reality: the bond of a large state of strangers, the principles of international relations among independent states, and the selection of the ruling members of the state and even the world. I have illustrated the Confucian answer to the third question, and argued why the mixed regime inspired by Confucianism can still be viable and address the crises of “democracy,” in another article. Here, I will focus on how Confucians answer the first two questions and why they offer a viable and even better alternative to the nation-state and cosmopolitan models that came out of Western modernity.

The Confucian moral ideal is universal but unequal love.

On the issue of a new social bond, Mencius, an important Confucian thinker (372-289 BCE), argued that all human beings have the sentiment of compassion, a sense of care toward strangers. He offered a famous thought experiment to show this. If you suddenly see a baby who is about to fall into a well, would you feel a sense of alarm and distress? It is a beautifully designed experiment for many reasons. It uses a baby that embodies innocence, rather than an adult who might have done something to deserve to die; it asks about our immediate rather than our calculated response (which makes the baby a perfect stranger); and it asks us how we feel, not what we will do. It is hard to answer “no” in this hypothetical case.

But Mencius also realized that this sentiment, though universal, is very fragile. In order for it to be strong enough to hold strangers together, it needs to be cultivated, and family is a universal and important institution in which this cultivation can take place. We take family as something private, but at the same time, family is the first place for us to transcend our mere self, when, for example, we are asked to save a piece of candy for our baby sister or the best seat for our grandma. This is why familial care is so important to Confucians. Confucianism is no philosophy of Don Corleone, the Godfather (“never go against the family”), as some critics have claimed. Rather, family is an institution where we learn to care about others by first learning to care about our family members. Confucian moral psychology argues that we care about the sufferings of strangers because they remind us of the sufferings of those closer to us. The expansion of care is continuous, and one should keep pushing our care outward, until it embraces every human being—living, not yet born, and dead—and also animals, plants, and things in the world. Family is our path to transcendence, and in this transcendence, the world of strangers is united.

But even at the stage of universal care, Confucians think that one still does and should care about the closer ones more than the more distant ones. Just imagine, even if you are this ideal person who has achieved universal compassion, who would you save first if your daughter and a stranger were drowning? In sum, the Confucian moral ideal is universal but unequal love.

Therefore, through compassion, the whole world can be bonded together, but at the same time, one is justified in caring more about one’s own state and people than other states and peoples. Patriotism is thus justified. But while caring about one’s own state first, being humane requires that one should not disregard the interests of other peoples completely. For example, if my state and another state are flooded, Confucians would reject the cosmopolitan idea that they should be treated equally, and would instead argue that I should try to save my own state first—but I shouldn’t do so by directing the flood to a neighboring state, a practice that a nationalist defender of their own nation-state may not object to.

Moreover, the Confucian argues, all humane states should form an alliance and play the role of world police that protect a civilized way of life. Being civilized means the preservation of the shared human heritage, such as the classics and historical statues and buildings, and treating all peoples humanely. These states should never go to war with each other because being civilized and compassionate requires never fighting against another state for material gains—that is an act of a beast. But if the people of another state suffers greatly from a bad regime, the alliance of civilized states should intervene, including using military force, although force has to be used cautiously and only as the last resort. Indeed, Mencius argued that only when a people suffers so greatly as to be ready to welcome the “invaders” can their liberation be carried out and justified. The Confucian world order is thus a humaneness-based hierarchy. It is different from the UN model where each state is treated equally, or where the five permanent members of the Security Council are the de facto dominant forces due to historical contingencies.

The principle beneath this world order is that humane duties, not human rights, override sovereignty. A state that treats its own people well, but emits a lot of carbon dioxide that exacerbates global warming and harms other peoples, is not fully humane and thus should not enjoy full sovereignty. This means that other states can legitimately intervene in the climate policies of this state. If a state doesn’t treat its own people well, and even puts them in desperate situations, the state loses its sovereignty completely, and liberation by other truly humane states can be justified.

Unlike cosmopolitanism—a radical version of liberalism, according to which everyone should be treated equally and states should eventually be abolished—Confucianism considers the existence of states legitimate, and the Confucian model puts a state’s own interests above those of other states. But unlike in the nation-state model, this priority is not absolute, and the legitimacy of a state is limited by how humanely it treats its own people and other peoples. Confucians would argue that the cosmopolitan model is too good to be true because it demands too much from human beings, while the nation-state model is too demeaning to human beings because it treats them as merely self-interest-driven animals. Thus, the Confucian model is more realistic than the cosmopolitan model, and more idealistic than the nation-state model. It is a “realistic utopia” that strikes a golden mean between the two. To put it differently, the Confucians realize that only states have power. International organizations cannot really impose their will on states, for covenant without sword is mere words, as Hobbes would put it. Until there is a united world government that has authority backed up with force, only states can enforce trans-state order. The only hope, then, is to tame the powerful states with humaneness.

How do we get there if this Confucian new “Tian Xia” order is truly desirable? A simple path is for the G2, the US and China, to take up the role of benevolent world police, which doesn’t seem likely now. Still, ASEAN, the EU, and other responsible great and middle powers can form alliances and offer public goods to all. I am not optimistic about this path, but it is the only realistic one for global order.

This article is an edited version of an article first published in Singapore-based Think China.
